sources.title: Not just when, but how: An exploratory dual-control approach to video feedback in motor learning

findings.finding: Allowing learners to choose when to watch video feedback of their movement improves movement form even without extra cueing.
findings.quote: Importantly, however, the results indicated that SC video feedback conferred a learning benefit without the provision of explicit additional attentional cueing.

findings.finding: Learner-controlled video self-observation boosts intrinsic motivation, perceived choice, self-efficacy, and physical skill progression compared to externally scheduled viewing.
findings.quote: Results of the retention test showed that the participants in the LC group obtained higher scores on the intrinsic motivation and perceived choice measures and had higher skill progression scores

findings.finding: Letting learners control both the timing of video feedback and interactive playback controls yields the strongest and most durable learning gains.
findings.quote: These findings suggest that interactive video tools may be most useful when learners can regulate both when feedback is accessed and how it is inspected.

principle: Learners acquire motor skills better and gain more self-efficacy when they decide for themselves when to review their video feedback and how to inspect it.
for_the_teacher: Let the learner decide when to trigger and watch a recorded video replay of their dancing rather than showing it automatically.
Provide interactive playback controls—such as pause, slow motion, and rewind—so the learner can inspect their recorded movement at their own pace.
when_it_does_not_apply: In pre-registration physiotherapy education, high fidelity simulation combined with video feedback did not improve motor skill performance and resulted in an increased number of safety fails compared to low fidelity controls.
